messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Shouting: Shouting, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Kofi

Kofi was fifty-five when the hurricane came. He had spent thirty years in bomb disposal—a career that had taught him to read silence, to move with precision through chaos, to keep his body and mind in perfect synchrony. He lived in New Orleans with his wife, Ama, in a modest house two blocks from the levee. When the storm warnings escalated that August morning, he had done what he always did: assessed the threat logically, made a plan, and told himself he could manage it. He was wrong.

The storm surge came faster than the meteorologists had predicted. Kofi and Ama had evacuated to a shelter in the Convention Center, but the building's integrity failed within hours. The roof began to fail in sections—a grinding, metallic shriek followed by a percussion of falling debris that echoed through the cavernous space. Kofi remembered the sound more vividly than he remembered his own breathing. He remembered the way the concrete floor shook, the way people screamed in a register he had never heard before, the way the darkness came in waves as sections of roof collapsed. He had grabbed Ama and pulled her toward what he thought was a safer corner, but in the chaos—the noise, the dust, the unpredictability of where the next collapse would come—he had lost her hand for forty-seven seconds. Forty-seven seconds in which he could not see her, could not reach her, could not protect her. When he found her again, she was crying, but she was alive. That was three years ago.

Since then, Kofi's world had contracted. The job he had excelled at for three decades—a profession built on his ability to remain calm in the presence of genuine danger—had become impossible. He had taken early retirement six months after the hurricane, unable to tolerate the unpredictability of the work, the sudden loud noises of equipment, the way his body would betray him without warning. But leaving the job had not brought relief. Instead, the absence of structure seemed to make everything worse. At home, he had begun to avoid anything that felt remotely stressful: he declined social invitations, stopped attending his church, refused to drive on highways where traffic was unpredictable. When Ama suggested they visit her sister in Houston, the thought of the drive—the uncontrolled variables, the other drivers, the possibility of something unexpected—sent his heart racing. He had said no, and when she pushed, he had shouted. Shouting, he had come to realize, was one of his triggers; the sound of his own raised voice could send him spiraling, could make his body brace as if the roof were failing again.

To manage the mounting distress, Kofi had developed routines. He kept his mind occupied constantly—audiobooks, podcasts, the endless scroll of news—anything to prevent silence or stillness. He overate, particularly in the evenings, consuming large meals or entire boxes of pastries in an attempt to soothe the anxiety that would otherwise consume him. These strategies provided temporary relief, but they also kept him trapped in a narrowing cycle. The more he avoided potential stressors, the more his world shrank, and the more his nervous system seemed to interpret ordinary situations as dangerous. A car horn outside would send his body into immediate alarm—his heart would race, his muscles would tense, his mind would flash to that moment in the Convention Center—before he had even consciously registered the sound. When Ama raised her voice to ask why he hadn't answered her question, his body reacted as if she were screaming in terror, and he found himself shouting back, which only deepened his shame and his need to retreat further into avoidance and distraction.

The memories themselves had become fragmented and overwhelming. Kofi could recall the sound of the collapse, the sensation of losing Ama's hand, the taste of dust in his mouth, but the sequence felt incomplete, as if crucial moments had been erased. When he tried to piece it together, to understand what had happened and why he could not move past it, rage would flood through him—a fury so intense that it frightened him. He had come to avoid thinking about that day altogether, pushing the memories away the moment they surfaced, which meant they never fully resolved. Instead, they lurked at the edges of his consciousness, ready to ambush him when a door slammed or when an unexpected noise pierced the quiet. His body would react before his mind could catch up, flooding him with the certainty that danger was imminent, that he was back in that collapsing building, that he might lose Ama again. This conviction—that threat was ever-present, that unpredictability meant danger, that his body's alarms were reliable—drove him deeper into avoidance. He avoided situations that might trigger memories, which meant he avoided the very unpredictability that, in his mind, had nearly cost him everything. And as he avoided, as he overate, as he kept his mind perpetually occupied, the triggers seemed to multiply. Ordinary sounds became threatening. His own emotional responses became unpredictable to him. He had begun to wonder if he would ever feel safe again.

It was Ama who finally insisted he seek help. She had noticed his weight gain, his social withdrawal, the way he would sometimes look at her as if he did not quite recognize her. She had also noticed the way he flinched at her voice, the way he seemed to be disappearing into himself. Three weeks ago, she had placed a therapist's business card on his nightstand and said, "I need my husband back." That simple statement—the recognition that he was losing something precious, that his strategies were costing him more than they were saving—had finally broken through his resistance. Kofi sat in the intake session with his hands folded, uncertain whether talking about what happened would make things better or infinitely worse, but aware that the alternative—this slow, suffocating contraction of his life—was no longer bearable.
